name: Alpine Style
camps: Single carry; bivouacs on the move
description: Climbing the mountain in a continuous single push from base to summit and back, carrying all food, fuel, and shelter on your back. No pre-established camps, no fixed ropes, no supplemental oxygen. Favors speed, minimal exposure time, and supreme technical elegance.
pros: Minimal exposure to objective hazards (avalanches, seracs)
No environmental litter left on slopes
Ultimate test of athletic endurance and skill
cons: Zero margin of safety if trapped by sudden storms
Carrying heavy technical packs on vertical pitches
representativeClimbers: Reinhold Messner, Steve House, Ueli Steck, Voytek Kurtyka

name: Expedition (Siege) Style
fixedRopes: Extensive (Kilometers of line from Base to High Camps)
description: A methodical military-style siege of a peak. Climbers establish a fortified Base Camp, ferry supplies up and down to acclimatize ('climb high, sleep low'), establish fixed ropes across technical passages, and wait for a stable weather window for the final summit push.
pros: Higher summit success probability for commercial clients
Stocked camps with safety caches, medical oxygen, and food
Fixed ropes reduce slip-and-fall fatalities on descent
cons: Protracted exposure to glacier movement and rockfall
Heavily dependent on high-altitude support teams

name: Capsule Style
camps: Portaledges or snow ledges moved upward as a pod
description: A hybrid method predominantly used on enormous vertical granite spires (e.g. Trango Towers, Patagonia). A small team establishes a 'capsule' camp on a high ledge or hanging portaledge, climbs 200-300 meters above it fixing short lines, then hoists the entire camp upward to start the next block.
pros: Enables ascents of extreme vertical rock faces in adverse weather
Low reliance on large external teams
cons: Physically punishing hauling of 60kg haul bags on vertical terrain
Confinement to small hanging ledges during multi-day blizzards
representativeClimbers: Big wall climbers in Karakoram and Patagonia
